utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We continue today with the hearing of evidence by way of video-conference link from Sarajevo. Mr. Whiting, anything to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's all right, Your Honour. Your Honour, I just want to tell the Court that, as I have alluded to a couple of times, we have been having difficulty with one witness, and I just want to tell you now that Witness 39 with will not be giving evidence, just for planning purposes. We have two witnesses for today, both of which will be taken by Mr. Sachdeva, and that will conclude our videolink evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let the witness make the declaration. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I just want to confirm that can you hear me in a language that you understand and that you can see me as well.

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes. I can hear you and I can see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: My name is Manoj Sachdeva and I'm a lawyer for the Prosecution, and I'm going to be ask you a few questions this morning. Can you start by stating your full name, your date, and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: My name is Nefa Sljivo, and I was born on the 9th of May, 1972 in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May I ask you, do you recall giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 8th of March, 1997?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you recall giving a further statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 27th of April, 2006?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in the last couple of days, did you meet with colleagues from the Tribunal and did they read out and show you those statements?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And upon reviewing and reading through those statements, are you able now to confirm the accuracy and the truth of the contents of those statements, to the best of your knowledge and recollection. I'm sorry. Witness, could you repeat your answer, please? I don't think it came through.

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that 65 ter 03069 be brought up on the screen and also shown to the witness in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see there in front of you a statement dated the 27th of April, 2006?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on the first page, do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you questions today, would the answers to those questions reflect the content of this statement?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that that statement be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P531, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could now ask for 65 ter 03070 to be brought up on the screen and also shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you see a statement there dated the 8th of March, 1997?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, again, on the first page, do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I were to ask you questions today in court, would your answers reflect the content of this statement?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this statements entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P532, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, I'm just going to ask you a couple of more questions. Firstly, the statement you gave to the Prosecutor pertained to an incident on the 1st of July, 1995, and I want to ask you: Did you sustain any injuries as a result of the incident on the 1st of July, 1995 in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes. Probably when the house fell down, parts of the wall, fragments of the wall, hit me in the back. I don't recall how many of these fragments there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can I ask you: As a result of those injuries, did you have to go to hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: When we left the house, we went to the outpatients' clinic where I was examined; after that, we went to the hospital. It was called the Enver Maric hospital, and there they established that my injuries were not very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that 65 ter 03075 be brought up on screen and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, in a moment I'm going to show you -- or the court officer in Sarajevo is going to show you a record. And I just want to you look at that record and tell the Court whether this is a record of your admission to the hospital that you just spoke about?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I ask that this medical record be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P533, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Lastly, Witness, on that day of the incident, the 1st of July, 1995, did you notice any military activity taking place in the vicinity of your residence or in that area?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I don't remember anything happening. I really can't remember whether anything happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Court whether in the vicinity of your residence there were any military objects or facilities nearby?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Near the house there was a house in which the observers were, the monitors. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say "observers," are you referring to -- well, actually, who are you referring to when you say "observers"?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: The UN observers, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. So I'll just be more clear in my question. Apart from the UN observers, were there any members of the Bosnian government military or military installations of the Bosnian government military near your location, near your house?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sachdeva. Now, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'm Branislava Isailovic. I'm a lawyer with the Paris Bar, and I'm representing General Dragomir Milosevic, the accused in these proceedings. I'm going ask you a few questions regarding these two statements that you made and that have you just dealt with with the Prosecutor. In your first statement, document 65 ter 03070, which has been given the number P532, this is a statement dated March 8, 1997, the first statement that you made to the Prosecutor's office. It's the first one you made, right?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement, you talk about an air bomb which fell on the television building. Can you see this statement, and I'm talking about paragraph 3 on page 2.

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Here you say that you heard about air bombs for the first time when one fell on the television building. Do you still agree with this? Do you maintain this?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then regarding the incident that is the topic today, which is July 1st, 1995, do you remember exactly how long it was since you heard about the air bomb that fell on the television building?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly how long it was, but I just remember that people said that an air bomb fell on the television building.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But was it the same year as the incident that occurred on July 1st, 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I think it was, but, believe me, so much time has elapsed. I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But where or how did you hear about this first incident? Was it through the media?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Well, yes, through the media. How else?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And what exactly did the media report regarding this bomb that fell on the TV building?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I can't remember that. The only thing I do remember is that it was an air bomb, because the same kind of bomb hit my house. I think it was the same kind of bomb.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: July 1st, 1995, there's been extensive damage to the house, but the first impact was on the roof of the house, right?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: It was in 1992. A shell landed in 1992; I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. That's in paragraph 2. But I'm talking about July 1st, 1995. Was your house directly hit by this bomb; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: The bomb hit the garage which was in front of the house and it was connected to the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This was the garage that belonged to your family?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement, in paragraph 4, you say that you heard a sound, and you say that at that time you knew it was mortar, something like that being fired. That's what you said, right?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Well, because I had been listening to those sounds for four or five years, so we could tell, more or less. But this one produced a horrible sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I'm asking the question. You had experience in 1995. You knew about this noise. So the noise you heard then, was it similar to the one you heard in 1992 when the mortar shell fell on your house?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: No, it was nothing like that. This sound was awful.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Horrible, horrible, or awful, but how was it awful? Because it was very loud? Could you describe what "awful" exactly means?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: The sound was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm listening to the French, but you said a special word in B/C/S. Could you repeat and say exactly what was awful for the transcript, so we know exactly what was so awful or so terrible in relation to this noise?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: The sound was much stronger, much louder than the ones I had heard before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, isn't it true that there were many such noises in Hrasnica and you heard many such sounds. You heard the sounds of many different weapons in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, because we were being targeted. So, yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: There were many soldiers of the ABiH army that were billeted in Hrasnica. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: In Hrasnica, we were defending ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You're thinking about the soldiers that were stationed in Hrasnica. They defended themselves?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And this is a neighbourhood in Sarajevo, but it's a little bit aside. It's located at the very foot of Mount Igman, right?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And very close to it. When you -- when you were in your house, Mount Igman is right there, right?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, behind it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And the Igman road is also -- goes also through the foot -- goes to the foot of Mount Igman and is parallel to the street where your house is located?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And this route can be -- this road can be used to climb up Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Well, probably. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You were a resident of Hrasnica. Do you remember that at the time there was a tunnel under the runway of the airport, and the entry -- entry or exit point was in Donji Kotorac? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At the time did you know that the tunnel was used by the ABiH army so soldiers would go up on Igman?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably. I know I used the tunnel to go to town, and people came to Hrasnica from town through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This is new to me. You personally took the tunnel several times to get into Sarajevo to the City Centre?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did. Because I, in 1995, became a student at the university, I had to use the tunnel to go to the university, although I lived at Dobrinja. But to reach Dobrinja, I had to use the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how often you used this tunnel at that period of time? We're talking about 1995, right?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Not often. I can't remember now, but it wasn't every day. Perhaps once a month, because I would come back to see my mother.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have to tell anyone about the fact that you wanted to use the tunnel? Did you have to tell someone in Dobrinja, for example, about it before taking the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: We went to the municipality to get passes to go through the tunnel. We as students were able to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So as a student, you were entitled to get this pass.

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And with the pass, you were allowed to go through the tunnel, to go towards the City Centre or to come back. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The people giving the pass, were they military or was it the civil servants at the municipality; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I didn't get the pass from the army. I got it from the civilian authorities, from the municipality, because I was a student.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And once you were -- once you were at the entry point to the tunnel, was that -- was it the soldiers or the army that were controlling the passes or was it civilian police? Do you remember exactly who did the check at the entry of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: The people wore suits; police, army. They all wore the same kind of clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That suit, was it a uniform or was it civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: They were uniforms, uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, I have one question for clarification, please. What fell on the garage next to your house? Was it an air bomb or was it a mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I was told that it was an air bomb which was not dropped from a plane but launched from I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were told it was an air bomb. But to your knowledge, was there an investigation made by the local police or by the UN forces or by any authority; and if so, do you know what the findings of this investigation were, as to the origin of the bomb?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: The police came that morning after the bomb fell, after it landed, and someone said they said it was an air bomb. I don't remember anything else. I know they did come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Witness. I would like --

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would like to put one short question to you relating to the passage through the tunnel. And if I understand you correctly, because your residence was outside the city and your university where you studied was within the city, the confrontation lines of the city, you sometimes passed through the tunnel when you wanted to move from the inner city to your home, your residence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's all right. I understand you to say that you were studying at the university which I suppose was located within the confrontation line; that is to say, in the city centre somewhere, yet your family was living outside. So in order to get from the university to your family residence, you would have to go through the tunnel, and you did so, as I understand, once --

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- every month, or so; and then you said that --

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's fine. But then you said that you could obtain a pass in order to go through the tunnel, and I understand that this pass was sort of a permission to pass through the tunnel. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you have to pay money in order to obtain that passport, or were the passports given free of charge because you were a student?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: No, I didn't pay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But did anyone have to pay? Do you know if anyone had to pay for a pass in order to pass through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were there any restrictions to your knowledge in the issuing of passes to civilians in order to go through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that people brought food to Sarajevo through that tunnel. Hrasnica was linked to Herzegovina via Igman. There was more food in our area than in Sarajevo, so people took food from our area into Sarajevo. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To your recollection, could people, civilians obtain a passport, a pass at any time without any restrictions in order to pass through the tunnel? In other words, do you know if there was a free passage for everyone as long as they just had a pass?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know that I, as a student, had a pass. I really don't know whether everyone could get through all the time. Since people knew that there was a tunnel there, it was targeted a lot, and people also knew that a lot of other people got killed there by the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But my questions relate to the issue of whether there was more or less free passage for everyone through the tunnel, and I understand your response to say that you don't know this?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that I, as a student, had this pass; otherwise, I wouldn't go to town. Had I not continued my studies, I simply wouldn't go there, because that was also exposure to, well...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if your pass was given to you because you were a student? In other words, were passes automatically given to all students?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I don't know about that. What was said was that students could go there and have this pass all the time. Now, whether everybody could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: One last question, and that is: Can you remember, roughly, if there were many people going with you through the tunnel at the times when you did it, or was it a limited number of people? In other words, could you roughly indicate the number of people who went through with you at those times? 50 people, 100 people, 500 people; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: I really cannot. I just know that you had to wait. You had to wait on one side when people would go through the other side, and then they would have to wait when we were going through. Perhaps around 50 or something. Believe me, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much, Madam Witness, and have a good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Ms. Sljivo, just one question. With respect to the tunnel entrance, can you tell the Court how far your house was from the entrance to the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: NEFA SLJIVO
utterances.text: Around four kilometres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it and you may not leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm informed by the court deputy that we need a 20-minute break to allow for the setting up of certain measures for the next witness. So we'll adjourn for 20 minutes. --- Break taken at 9.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration -- sorry. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Let us hear from Ms. Isailovic first before the witness makes the declaration. So, Witness, you will have to wait for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It's just a question I wanted to raise this morning. My client told me about a few problems he has with transportation, especially these days when we are having a schedule which is bit different from the other days. And he has transportation extremely early and then he has to wait an extremely long time after the hearing before being transferred back. This is what happened yesterday and the day before yesterday. The waiting rooms here are quite uncomfortable. There is no heating. I go there very often, and it is very unpleasant to have to wait there more than 20 minutes. He is -- yesterday he to wait for two hours for transportation which is extremely unpleasant. So I wanted to tell the court about this, if the Chamber has the possibility of raising the question to the competent department in order to remedy this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber shares the concern that you have expressed on behalf of the accused with regard to the arrangements for his transportation. He should not have to wait two hours, and I will instruct the court deputy to pass this on to the registrar, and the registrar will, I'm sure, see to it that there is an improvement in transportation for the accused. Is that all, Ms. Isailovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language that you understand, and can you see me also on the screen there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Yes. I can here you but I cannot see you on the screen, oh, and there's this woman's voice that I hear, she's talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, my name is Manoj Sachdeva and I'm one of the lawyers for the Prosecution, and I am going to ask you a few questions. Firstly, to inform you, you had requested protective measures so as to withhold your identity to the public, and the Court has granted those measures. So in a moment, I am going to ask -- well, in fact, now I am going to ask the court deputy down in Sarajevo to show you a piece of paper; and on --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: -- that piece of paper, there should be your personal details, and I would like you to confirm to the Court that those are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have copy for the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And I'm going to refer to you as Witness 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move that pseudonym sheet into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be P534, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Witness 13, do you remember giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 10th of March, 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in the last couple of days, did members of the Tribunal give you an opportunity to read through that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: After that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. Within the last couple of days in Sarajevo, did members of the Tribunal give you an opportunity to read through your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And upon reviewing and reading through your statement, can you now confirm that the contents of that statement are accurate and truth, to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could now ask for 65 ter 03056 to be shown to the witness and to be brought up on the screen here but not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 13, do you see a statement there dated the 10th of March, 1997?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And on the first page, do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you questions today in court, would your answers reflect the content of that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember -- well, I don't know. We'll see. You know what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you this, Witness 13. Can you just confirm that what's in the statement that you gave on the 10th of March, 1997 is indeed correct and accurate, to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Yes. All of it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I offer this statement into evidence, under seal. I would just note in the 92 application for this statement the Prosecution asked for the final four paragraphs in the English version to be admitted into evidence. That is because the initial part of the statement was deemed to be not relevant to the case at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes P535, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness 13, in the statement that has just been admitted, you speak about an incident on the 26th of May, 1995, and I want to ask you: At the time --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps we can move into private session for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Isailovic, my plan was to stop at ten to before breaking, so that we would have made up for the 20-minute break we had earlier. But I would continue beyond that time for another five minutes, if you would be finishing, so please let me know. If not, we'll take the break in three or four minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just have a few questions to put to the witness. I think that the remaining seven minutes will suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We will continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember whether there were any dead people following this explosion on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: There weren't any dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And according to what you remember, and according what you know and found out after the incident, in those flats that were located in the building on which the bomb fell, were there any people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I didn't go into other peoples' flats, thinking I would be a witness one day. But in the course of the day when I came back from hospital, and on the following day, I did hear that on the last floor there was a woman who had a small baby. How true this was I cannot guarantee. But I heard that at the time of the explosion, it went through to the second floor and that this lady with a baby was alive and well, but the little girl's eardrums were damaged. But that was just rumours going around the neighbourhood, you understand. There weren't any people killed. There was some people injured, just as I had been. And there was a neighbour of mine. His son was a policeman. He was injured and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, as you were outside, did you actually see this bomb when it fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What did you hear, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: As I was on the fifth floor, thousands and thousands of shells landed in Sarajevo; and most of those shells, when they landed, you could hear a whistling sound. I don't have my teeth so I can't whistle properly, but I will try. The sound was like this ... and then suddenly there would be an explosion. You understand. But this bomb that I survived, I was facing the building with -- my right side was towards the building where the bomb fell, and I just heard as if there had been a helicopter some 15 metres above the buildings flying low. It was a sound different from the sound made by the other shells that landed in Mojmilo and Svrakino Selo, and then I heard an explosion and an impact on the right-hand side. My little Lejla was taking a bath. I thought it was -- I thought the bomb had landed on our building, so I called out to her, "Lejla, Lejla." I came to the entrance where I found some 20 people who were sheltering in the doorway from the detonation. They moved there instinctively. You understand. At that point, this journalist arrived, who I mistook for an UN soldier. At the same time, my little daughter Lejla ran down the stairs shouting, "Daddy, daddy." She put her arms around my waist and felt blood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think have you answered the question. Any more questions, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: One last question: Do you perhaps remember how long you heard this sound for, this strange sound? How long were you able to hear it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: I think about three or four seconds, not more. It could have been less, but not more, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I understood your statement correctly, the bomb fell on the fifth floor of the building, and the three last --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Yes, the roof was flat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- floors in the building were destroyed. Is that right? I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: The roof of the building was a flat roof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was an air bomb, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm an expert for those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were wounded, of course. The person whom you took for an UN soldier, who was in fact a journalist, came to help you. But do you know whether the Bosnian authorities or whether the United Nations representatives came to that location or not? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-13
utterances.text: Well, there was some sort of inspection, investigation. They investigated the depth of the crater and so on. I'm no expert in these matters. I was just an eye-witness when the bomb exploded. I can tell you where I was, but I cannot tell you whether it was air bomb or a 120 or an 82. I don't want to lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, no. But if I may, I would just like to inform the Court in response to His Honour Judge Mindua's question that Witness 138 did indeed testify about a police investigation into this incident, and the relevant records have been admitted into evidence. Other than that, no questions for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, I understand that we will also be leaving, Mr. Sachdeva, there being no other witness in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will therefore adjourn until Tuesday, the 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of April, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.56 a.m.,
